utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning, everybody. I see that all the accused are here. Mr. Haynes is not here Ms. Condon is not here. Otherwise we are a full house. Mr. McCloskey is behind the column; Mr. Nicholls is ready for action. I understand you have some preliminaries to raise and discuss. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. I have three issues I would like to raise this morning before this witness appears. The first one is not related to the witness but just in case we go right up to the end I would like to raise it at this time, this way we don't have to end early because we have no idea how long this witness will last. This issue has to deal with the -- a motion which was filed by the Defence of Drago Nikolic and that was a Defence request for review of the Registrar's decision and that was filed in December of last year. Now, the Registrar responded and filed a registry submission on the 22nd of January. Due to the contents of that submission we would like to file also some observations on the Registry submission. So we'd just like to ask permission because we feel that what the Registrar has done is not rules per se so we figure the best would be to ask your permission and we'll do this by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate your reply to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not very long. Not very long. Nothing more than the normal motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Permission granted. The other preliminary. The possible such matters can be dealt with without making use of Court time, if you -- there are many ways and means of doing this exercise otherwise. Yeah, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next issue concerns the next two witnesses that we will hear. There's been a change of course in the witness schedule. I believe the Trial Chamber is aware that the next two witnesses are witnesses we will testify with the -- under protective measures and maybe I should move into closed session to discuss my next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Nicholls. In your briefing of this witness, did you yourself, or whoever interrogated him, interviewed him, explain to him his rights under Rule 90 (E) or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Your Honour, and I told him it was likely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he's aware. In other words, I'm asking you so that we don't waste much time in explaining --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, any time you need to walk out and have a short rest, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence as a Prosecution witness. Our rules require that before you start testifying you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your undertaking that you will be speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Now, the Prosecution has asked us to put in place some protective measures to hide your identity, protect your identity. We have must these protective measures in place. Basically these are face and voice distortion. People outside will not be able to see your face or to hear your voice. Are you satisfied with this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before you start giving evidence we have been discussing here, particularly considering your occupation at the time of the conflict in 1995, to draw your attention to a particular disposition of our law, which gives you the right to object to making any statement or answering any question which you've answered truthfully might tend to incriminate you. If you do not make such a request, then you are bound to answer the question. But if you make such a request, then it's up to us to decide whether to grant you your request and exempt you from answering such questions or whether to compel you to answer the question. In other words, the Trial Chamber has the discretion, the right to tell you, notwithstanding your request, we still want you to answer this question. However, therefore legal consequences which go to your benefit if you are compelled to answer such questions by the Trial Chamber. In such a case if you have compelled to answer such questions your testimony or that part of the testimony shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent Prosecution against you for any offence or further from any offence, unless of course the conclusion is that you have given false testimony. In that case, your answer would be taken into consideration, but only if you are charged with perjury, with false testimony. Otherwise, any answer you may give because you are compelled by the Trial Chamber to give, may not be made use of in your regard in any subsequent proceedings, prosecution against you. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think, having said that, I leave you in the very capable hands of Mr. Nicholls. He will then be followed by cross-examination. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm handing you a sheet of paper and I want you to read it silently to yourself; do not read it out loud. And the question I have for you is does your name appear on that sheet of paper, which will be P02404 under seal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If that could be shown to my colleagues. Sir, I have a few questions for you this morning and could we begin in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. And may I remind you to switch off your microphones when the witness is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, witness, I'm going to ask you some questions about what happened and what you remember after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. First of all, do you recall the date when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. It was mid-July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after that date were you ever ordered to guard Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you ever sent to do that duty in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would appreciate if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon me, Mr. Bourgon. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please show the witness on e-court 1690.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, there should be a photograph appearing on the screen in front of you now. It's got ERN number 0040-9643 along the top right. Can you just take a look at that photograph for a minute and tell me if you recognise the place in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes, this is the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for the record, which place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The elementary school in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that. Now, before you were sent to the elementary -- before you went to the elementary school in Orahovac? Did you know that was your destination? Did you know that's where you were going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can describe what appeared to be happening at -- at the school in Orahovac when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: When we arrived there our commander explained to us that prisoners would be coming that we needed to prepare the entrance gate, there was a gym there, and that's what we did. There was some wire there, it had already existed there, so it was used to delineate the area for them. And then after sometime, I don't know exactly how much time elapsed, civilian buses started arriving. Escorted by civilian police in blue uniforms, prisoners started coming off the bus and we escorted them into the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said that the wire was used to delineate the area for them, for the prisoners. Can you describe a little bit more what the function of this wire was, what was there for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The wire was there to create a passage for them, a corridor. Since this was a school, there was already a wire there in place, some five to six metres high, because there was a school playground. And I guess the wire was there in order to prevent the children from breaking a window when they played with a ball. And then we used this wire for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the school, were there any VRS soldiers already present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Leading question, Mr. President. He could ask was anybody there, but to ask whether there were VRS soldiers there is a leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day that's where we're going to get, Mr. Bourgon. I appreciate objecting to leading questions where they are of significant -- the objection is of significance, but not in this case, I suppose. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can the answer the question, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: A couple of soldiers of some sort, but we were there, military policemen, to secure the area, and there was already -- there were some people there who had already gathered out of curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe what you mean by the people who had gathered there out of curiosity and -- and the -- describe the soldiers that you say were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Well, at the time everybody wore military uniforms, so the houses where people lived were close by as well and people could see that something was going on and then their number grew to the size of a crowd once the buses started arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able to tell which units any of these other soldiers present belonged to, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: There were both local residents there and people moving through in transit, because this was the road leading to defence lines in Kitovica [phoen] and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was were other soldiers at the school, and you said there were a couple of some sort. Were you able to tell -- if you were, which military units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Well, I recognised a couple of people. They were drivers in the Zvornik Brigade. I used to see them frequently because they had been stationed in that barracks for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, without -- you talked about the buses. How long -- if you remember, how long after you got there did the buses start arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Well, soon thereafter; half an hour, an hour, they started arriving after that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the bus companies, if there were any names on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: A couple of names; Drinatrans, Vihor, Milici. Different buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And approximately how many buses arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: A dozen or more, I think. I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there any escort provided for these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. A policeman wearing blue uniforms, civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened after these buses started arriving? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: They went through the corridor that we had prepared for them and started entering the gym. We started taking them inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, I object to that question. Non-responsive. Unless the bus where is taken inside the school. The questionable is non-responsive and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well let's put a second question to clarify exactly what went into the school or went into the gym or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to do that and I think it's pretty hyper-technical objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you say, "They went through the corridor that we had prepared for them and started entering the gym" who is the "they" that you are referring to? Who went to the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Prisoners from buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Best you recall, how were these prisoners dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Different kinds of clothing. Pretty poor and shabby clothing, if I can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how full was the gym once all of the prisoners had entered it? ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: It was full. We left an area the size of two to four metres from the entrance, we left that area vacant so that we could control them better. The rest of the gym was completely full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about a crowd forming and coming from the houses, different people. What were they doing, what was their attitude towards the prisoners in the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Hostile, aggressive. There was huge commotion, confusion there. People milling about. There were only five or six of us military policemen, and it was difficult to control the crowd. As I said, people were mostly from the area, locals who had come there out of curiosity, and then I also realised that there were people in transit who were on their way to defence lines and stopped there to see what was going on. Everybody wanted to go in to see them, to give some comments and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And without saying the name of the person --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Comments of -- along the lines, "All of them ought to be killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And without saying the name of the person who gave you orders, what -- what were your specific duties at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: To secure the facility and provide security to prisoners to stop the crowd from getting to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't given an indication of how big or the size of this crowd. Perhaps you can ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You heard His Honour's query. Can you give us some idea of how big this crowd of people were who you say were aggressive and hostile towards the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I never thought about that, but about 100 people or so, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you successful in preventing the crowd from reaching or in any way harming the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. With great difficulty, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in addition --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In addition to the commander who you say gave you orders, and I won't say his name again, when you arrived at the school, can you tell me if you saw any other officers from the Zvornik Brigade there that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: May I give the name? Yes, I did. Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did you see Drago Nikolic at the school in Orahovac that day, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours. Between 12.00 and 2.00 or 3.00 p.m. I wouldn't be able to say, because we were quite busy. All of us military policemen there were busy with the prisoners, escorting them. And I saw him standing on the road separate from the crowd or the column passing through, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was he doing when he was standing on the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Talking. There were a lot of soldiers there, as I told you, on their way someplace else, who stopped there. Us military policemen, or rather I knew some of them by sight, and -- but I didn't know all of them, and we just started talking among ourselves and based on their conduct we concluded that these were senior officers and that he was talking to them about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, other than that occasion where you saw Drago Nikolic talking to these senior officers, are there any other times during the day that you saw Drago Nikolic at the school in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Maybe another two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was he doing on those other two times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The same. He didn't go in, nor did he approach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions now about the prisoners at the school. Did you observe any mistreatment or -- sorry. How were the prisoners treated, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: We let them go fetch water. We were unable to provide proper or good conditions, or if I can call it normal conditions, because this was not a normal situation [Realtime transcript read in error, "this was a normal situation"]. But they did go to fetch water. Nobody mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And best you can recall, how long did the prisoners stay? I think my friend has a -- has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, something in the transcript. Here we read on page 24, line 18 says, "Because this was a normal situation," I think it's completely different from what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me read your answer as we have it in the transcript, witness. And then hoping that it will be translated into your language as it is. Please give us your answer again. "We let them go fetch water. We were unable to provide proper or good conditions or if I can call it normal conditions, because this was a normal situation. But they go d go to fetch water. Nobody mistreated them". Did you ever say that this was a normal situation? Or did you say exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. Does it satisfy you, Mr. Lazarevic? Okay. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was starting to ask you, best you can remember how long did the prisoners remain in the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: In the afternoon, sometime in the afternoon. They stayed a few hours after they arrived they -- they were there for a few hours and we were securing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now about how the prisoners came to leave the school that day. Can you describe that, please, the process of how the prisoners left the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: A truck came. If I can say it like that, the exit from the gym was somewhere in the middle. We were all of us at the entrance, and when we were all inside I didn't even know that this exit existed until the truck came into which they were loaded, boarded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether it was a military or civilian truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you describe the process of how the prisoners, as you say, were loaded or boarded on to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The truck would park, it would come to the exit, there were three or four of us military police officers at the entrance we felt people were needed there. Two military police officers were there and maybe one or two soldiers and the driver. It wasn't a very large group around that truck. Four or five people and they were boarded on to the truck with their hands tied. That's how they were loaded on to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you remember, who tied the hands of the prisoners when they were loaded on to the trucks? And I don't mean the name of the person or persons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. They were either members of the military police or those people. I don't really know. I was looking over there at the entrance, because the crowd would start getting agitated when they started to bring them out, because they didn't know where they were taking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened after the prisoners were loaded on to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: It would drive out of the schoolyard and turn right. I know that that was the direction of Tuzla and towards our line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened? Continue telling about the process of how the prisoners were removed from the school, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The truck would come back shortly afterwards, you could hear shots, and then it would do the same thing again, it would come up to the school, into the schoolyard, once again people were loaded in, driven away, and this went on until the place was emptied, until it was almost dark, until all the people were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe the shots you heard? How many shots, how often you heard the shooting, and which direction that you could hear those shots coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: From the direction that they were taken you could hear the firing, the bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At any time during this process or cycle you've described, did any -- did any people come and talk about what has happening down the road in the direction the prisoners had been taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. There was always a couple of people running after or next to the truck, people in uniform, one or two military police officers and then on one of the return trips I heard them saying that they had been killed, executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a bit of a silly question, but just to keep the record very clear, who had been killed, executed? Who is the "they" there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The prisoners who had been taken away in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you personally ever go up to the road to where the shots were coming from and from where you heard that the prisoners were being killed? Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The people in uniform or military police officers who came back and said that the prisoners had been killed, were you able to tell which unit they belonged to, if you were able to tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The military police officers were from the Zvornik Brigade, and the rest of the soldiers were from that brigade, because I could see that they knew the local population. But as I said, it was uncontrolled. Anyone could come up to the column and come up behind the truck. It was only the duty of the police to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to clarify, because I'm not sure, I'm not that fluent in B/C/S, but I'd like to confirm whether he said police officers or police soldiers, to the best of my ability, he said police soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not have that much ability. So I will -- as you have, Mr. Bourgon, so I will ask the witness to explain. In answering Mr. Nicholls's question, Witness, according to the transcript you said, "The military police officers were from the Zvornik Brigade, and the rest of the soldiers were from that brigade." Is this a correct translation of what you said or do you wish to correct it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that is correct. But I would like to correct myself. Perhaps it wasn't the duty of the military police officers to go with the truck. I only saw them with the truck at one time, but the rest were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, after all the prisoners had been taken from the school, what happened with you next? What did you do, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember precisely how long we remained there. I don't know if I slept in the barracks overnight or if I stayed there until late into the night. I really don't remember. I don't remember, or perhaps I went home, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before going further, if you could clarify this. Earlier to your question, "Who tied the hands of the prisoners when they were loaded on to the trucks," the witness answered that, "They were either members of the military police or those people." If you could clarify who "those people" were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And perhaps could we go into private session just for this out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the events you have described at the Orahovac school, what was your next duty? What was the next task that you were ordered to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The following day we went to a school, it was also a school, in a placed call Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you told, or did you know that you were going to the Rocevic School when you left the barracks? Were you told that in advance that was destination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that we were transferred, myself and a couple of other policemen, to go to the school in Rocevic. (redacted) told us to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Request a redaction, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, line 16 on page 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will redact the name of the officer. And let's proceed. If you need to go into private session, please, you only have to ask, Mr. Nicholls, but I don't think it's the case of going into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, were you told what your duties would be at the Rocevic School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Securing the facility and the same thing that we were doing the day before at Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that? Just the same thing you were doing the day before at Orahovac, could you be more specific for the record? I think it's clear, but we need to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Specifically securing the facility and the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What time of day was it or what time was it, day or night, that you left to go to the Rocevic School?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: It was day. It was day; 10.00 or 11.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you please describe when you -- when you got to the school at Rocevic, what did you see there, what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The prisoner were already in the school, in the gym also. I saw a couple of bodies, dead bodies lying around. We were immediately assigned, because there also people wanted to come, there were a lot of angry people. Somebody had lost somebody in the war, and so it was, "Oh, let me come in and kill someone." There were things being said like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The bodies that you saw lying around the school, can you describe those bodies, what kind of clothing you saw on those bodies and -- well, that's it to start.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Civilian clothing. Somebody was perhaps wearing a camouflage shirt or trousers, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you able to tell what the ethnicity of the -- of these bodies were, whether they were Serbs or Muslims that were lying there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Muslims, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how do you conclude that? How could you tell that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Well, you didn't need much time to reach that conclusion. I simply knew. I saw who the people were, what they were, the bodies were later taken into the truck and transported together with the live prisoners who were later taken to the place of execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to tell at all, or make an estimate of how many prisoners there were in the Rocevic School when you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: It was a gym more or less of the same size as the one in Orahovac, I'm not sure. I would just glance inside and I think that the number was -- of people was the same as the number in the school in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you able to tell which unit or units, soldiers guarding the prisoners there, were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: We were there, the military policemen, two or three of us, military policemen and the rest were, I think, members of the Zvornik Brigade. There were no people from the outside. And the local population. It was hard to control it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After you arrived, just speaking about after you arrived, were you able to -- were you successful at keeping the crowd from harming the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes, we were. At least I think we were. But how can you say it? A person would come with weapons, they would be drunk or sober, but in a rage; I mean, it was difficult to deal with people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So upon the suggestion of Mr. Nicholls, we will have a 25-minute break starting from now and then he will -- when we resume he will conclude his direct. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. We are in open session and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to now describe how the prisoners came to leave the Rocevic School. Can you discuss that process, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: They were boarded into a truck, the same way as in Orahovac. Based on the stories I heard, they were taken to Kozluk where there was a dump, and later on there were stories circulating, and it was an open secret that this is where they executed them, shot them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many trucks were there picking up the prisoners, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but it wasn't a low number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as best you can remember, once a truck -- once trucks left, how long was it before new trucks came to pick up the prisoners? In other words, you described the cycle at Orahovac, can you describe at Rocevic, how long it took for each truckload of prisoners to be transported away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Here the destination was further away, the trip between Rocevic and Kozluk was about a 20-minute trip. About 20 minutes, but to tell you the truth, I didn't have a watch on me then, and at that time I simply lost any sense of time or area, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As far as you can recall, emptying the prisoners from the school of Rocevic and taking them away, did it take the same amount of time as at Rocevic or more or less? At Orahovac, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, do you mean approximately the same amount of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The same amount of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when was it that you left the school of Rocevic? Can you describe that, how you came to leave the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: It was near the evening when all of that was over, and when the room where they had been was vacant. After that we were taken to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you notice when the trucks were leaving whether they were accompanied by any escort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zivanovic, who is appearing for accused Popovic will be cross-examining you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to the crowd of civilians that you described who were in front of the school in Orahovac. Let me ask you this: You did not know these people previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So everything you heard from them about fury towards the prisoners you heard that while were you on duty in front of the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe in greater detail the nature of their fury at the prisoners at the school? Why were they furious at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: The main reason was that it was wartime. And this is how they viewed the enemy side. In addition to that, there were many people there who had lost their loved ones and that's the only way I could explain their hostility and hatred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was mostly people who had suffered losses in wartime, say they had lost their child or a brother or something like that? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Well, such individuals stood out from the crowd, yes. But there were also people there who were simply curious or who happened to be there accidentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they exposed -- expressed certain aggression, they wanted to settle scores with those prisoners, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement the one that I read, it says that some of them were even armed. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Everybody was armed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain something else to me, please. Since the prisoners were there inside the school, did they see them as members of the Muslim army or some paramilitary units? Is that how they perceived them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the same be said -- I don't want to repeat the question. Could the same be said of the situation in the village of Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will point out to -- a minor difference in relation to your previous statement. You said that when the buses arrived with prisoners there were a dozen or more of them. In your previous statement you said that there were about 10 of them. Perhaps it doesn't seem like a major difference to you; I just wanted to clarify. A dozen or more, that's what you said here. This "or more," could this mean one or two more or 10 to 20 more? I just want to narrow down this term that you used "or more." What could that possibly mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Listen, it wasn't my role to count the buses, nor was I able to do that. Because as they got off a bus we would escort them to this location and when I said "or more" that means that there could have been 15 of them, but not more than that. However, this is just my personal assessment; that doesn't need to be necessarily accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you rule out the possibility that there could have been less, that there could have been eight or nine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic who is appearing for Mr. Beara will be cross-examining you next.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have a few questions for you. I want to follow up on Mr. Zivanovic's question in relation to your statement. Do you recall when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question? I apologise, I didn't quite understand your question (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell me when it is that you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: In 2005, winter-time. End of year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have it here as being November 24th, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Nicholls, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. Just out of a huge abundance of caution, could we redact line 18, because that's a semi-unique quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's participate in this abundance of precaution and redact the line 18, or the last part starting from even the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, November 24th, 2005, is what I have on the statement sheet. Is that approximately accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Could you share with us, sir, how it is that you became a witness to give an interview 10 and a half years after the events of July of 1995 to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I was contacted by a police inspector from the Zvornik security station telling me that people from The Hague OTP were looking for me from the investigator's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did this occur, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Before I met up with the investigator, some 10 to 15 days prior to that. I'm not quite sure, maybe even less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a subpoena or a notice to appear to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Only from the police inspector. It was a verbal notice. He told me this in a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just briefly, Your Honours, if we can go into private session so I can have the name of the inspector, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a short while. Yes, Mr. Nicholls. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, where did you meet the Prosecutor to give your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: In the police station in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were any other former Zvornik Brigade military policemen also giving interviews on or about the date of November 24th, 2005?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This whole line is totally irrelevant and I think it's not the proper questions for him to put to the witness, which other people may or may not have been met. He can ask us this information any time he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct, but I think the witness also is in the position to give a very simple answer to that question. Can you give an answer to that question -- can you answer that question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about myself, I can't tell you anything about others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I anticipated hearing. So let's move ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, during the interview with the Office of the Prosecutor did they tell you that you were considered to be a witness or a suspect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't even remember that. I just know that they took a statement from me, I signed the statement. I think that I was told that I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During that interview, did they read any rights to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us what rights the Prosecutor read to you during your interview with them in November of 2005.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I remember that I was told when I signed the statement that it could be used in trials or in testimonies, in local courts. As for my own rights, I don't even remember whether they told me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember if the interview meeting in November 2005 was tape-recorded or video-recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I saw that both investigators were writing things down and there was a lap top in front of them. I didn't see any other devices there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long did the interview last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Three to four hours with a break. The break was about one hour long, after which they read my statement to me and prepared for me to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, sir, did the Prosecutor discuss all the events of July of 1995, or did they selectively discuss the events that you have testified during your direct examination here today and as reflected in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: These events. We discussed that period of time while I was in the military police. This is what it was about, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: (redacted). I simply wanted to clarify, to explain my stay in the military police. During that brief period of time I told them where I was, where I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct to understand that you personally did not witness any executions [Realtime transcript read in error, "excuses"], correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, am I also correct that in the school of Orahovac you did not see any dead bodies while you were, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What's -- Mr. Nicholls, what's the -- what's the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's no objection, I just ask to redact lines 25 and page 46, line 1. I didn't go into that unit in my direction and open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct. Let's redact those two lines, line 25 of page 45 and line 1 of page 46, please. Yes, in the meantime you may proceed, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on 46, just for correcting the record, on line 6 it shows, witness any excuses, but I think I said "executions," which -- just so it's clear, and I'm sure it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In any event, my last question to you, Mr. Witness and Your Honours, as I stated am I also correct that in the school of Orahovac, you did not see any dead bodies while you were there, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Stojanovic who is appearing for Borovcanin will be cross-examining you next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. Today during examination-in-chief on page 18, lines 15 through 18, you said that civilian buses started arriving and that they were escorted by civilian police in blue uniforms. Do you remember saying that today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to put several questions to you about this part of your evidence. How did the police in blue uniforms arrive? In what means of transportation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: They got off the buses. They were the first one to get off the buses. There were a couple of policemen on each bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those blue uniforms looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Blue police overalls, combat ones. Not the uniform that you wear when on patrol duty, no. These were blue combat overalls. Some of them were armed and some had flak jackets. Some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many there were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: They assisted us. As the buses arrived they got off the buses and then they worked together with us in that area. Where we worked with prisoners, there were perhaps seven to eight, maybe even 10 civilian policemen, because there were five to six of us military policemen, so there was simply no room for more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they go together with those buses and then come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes, they would come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify something. It seems we have a problem in the transcript. So they went together with buses and did not return back. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They went before the truck arrived, the truck that took the prisoners away, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these policemen at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't know. Some faces seemed familiar, yes. But I didn't really look at them intently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise them from the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Who is next? Madam Fauveau who is appearing for General Miletic will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have in questions -- we have no questions Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Defence team for General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same for us, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Defence team for Pandurevic, General Pandurevic. Okay, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what you said, Mr. Sarapa, if you could switch on and repeat what you said, please, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I said just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, then go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please specify, if you can, if you remember what was the date you were in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please, needs to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will -- we will do that, Mr. Sarapa. However, the interpreters have draw our attention that you need to raise your voice a little bit because they can barely hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and we have in private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Mr. Bourgon. Any time you need to go into private session, please advise us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness -- or good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you to clarify some parts of your testimony here today. And I will begin with the fact that -- and I guess I need to go into private session for my first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, you just -- in responding to my last question you referred to those vehicles. My question is more the total atmosphere as you are living these events, when you are trying to fend off, to use your number, you said there was 100 or so people there and you have a number of prisoners that have been taken into that school. That situation, maybe I can use the word "chaotic"; would that be a fair description?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes, that would be an -- a fair description.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, now I -- I take it -- I take this from your statement, this is not something you have mentioned today, but from your statement - and if there is a need I will show you your statement but I don't think that will be required - you mentioned that you were performing mostly crowd-control duties and that your attention was focused on the crowd. That's where you -- your main attention was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also in your statement, and now you gave this information as part of your testimony also today, you mentioned that you concluded that there were some higher officers who showed up that day during these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you yourself are not able to conclude either who they are or how high they are, but others around you came to such conclusions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. Amongst us military policemen, all I know are the people from the Zvornik Brigade, and a policeman kind of said yes, these are officers, and by the behaviour of Drago Nikolic you could see they were of superior rank. We commented amongst ourselves, but I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in respect to your last question -- or last response - sorry - brings exactly what I wanted to ask you, in terms of that when you saw Drago Nikolic speaking to those officers, you could not tell, you did not hear what was said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you can tell how he behaved that he was speaking indeed to higher officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, something that you said this morning at page 22, lines 7 to 9, which my understanding from what you said is that you actually saw the prisoners in the school at some point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes. I was at that entrance and occasionally I would just glance at it and check, because there was an empty space around us that we had left like that for our own and for their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we have some information that was reported to us by other people that there was some kind of a leader in there wearing a red beret. Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But are you in the position to confirm that those people who were directing the operations inside the gym, they were not from the Zvornik Brigade; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Could you please say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do. My question is simply that the people who are directing the operations inside the gym, I suggest to you that these people, unlike those that you described that were involved just outside, these people inside, they were not from Zvornik Brigade. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: No. All I remember are the military policemen. I don't know who you are talking about when you talk about those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But are you in a position to say because you answered earlier this morning when you referred to "those people," those people are people in addition to the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Those people, I said those people were near the truck when people were being boarded and transported away, the prisoners, and not in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, while you were in the gym, for that short period of time, you did give water to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: We let one of the prisoners go out to take water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next event that you testified about is, as my colleague referred to it, how the prisoners were -- came about to leave the gym. My question is straightforward in the sense of, until you heard from people around you talking about executions, after hearing some shots fired, until that very moment you never knew that there would be killings involved with those prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move on to -- well, no, one last question before moving to Rocevic. And that is a question that was asked to you by my colleague, but it was done in -- in private session. And I would like you to confirm now at this point that you felt ashamed as to what was going on but really there was nothing you could do. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you've already answered the question to fact that you were there until the last of the prisoners were taken out. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm curious, is during that time that you spent in the -- in this area - we're talking about a few hours according to your testimony - whether you saw -- whether anybody brought you food, either for you or for the detainees. Did you eat anything that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember any other vehicle coming to the school that day to bring some food to the people involved, and that is either the detainees or yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the people that -- the length of the people -- sorry, the duration of the stay of the prisoners in the gym, you already said that they spent a few hours, and that was in response to a prior question. My question to you is, I would suggest that those prisoners, the first who were taken out to be taken to the site where the killings took place, that this happened towards -- or later in the afternoon. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move on to Rocevic. And you've already testified, I'm not sure, so I will ask you this question, that Rocevic took place the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also I'd like you to confirm that the prisoners were already there and that the task which was assigned to you was the same one as in Orahovac, namely that was crowd control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, even though the previous day some prisoners, even though you didn't see it, you know that some prisoners were killed the previous day, on that day in Rocevic when you are doing your crowd-control duties, can you confirm that once again you did not expect the prisoners to be taken out to be killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the -- you described the situation at the Rocevic School, you mentioned that there were a very few of you from the military police, but there were other people with VRS military uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in response to a question from my colleague you mentioned that you did not -- you were not sure whether these people were from the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not objecting, but if my colleague has a reference, I'd like to have it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will provide a reference, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you be specific, yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is at -- I know it's on page 36, so I will just ... Okay. I refer my colleague to page 34 - I'm sorry - to line 16 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on this occasion, Witness, you mentioned that there was only two or three of us, I will not say what type of people we are talking about, but the rest you say "I think members of the Zvornik Brigade." And my question is you cannot say today that these people were indeed from the Zvornik Brigade; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Most of the people were locals, local people who were in uniforms. Well, I can say of course, yes, they're all members of the Zvornik Brigade, but they were wearing uniforms. Faces that were not familiar to me. I saw that there were many local citizens in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is simply you can't confirm from which unit these people were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I would simply like to get your -- your testimony on whether we can -- when we look at the situation in Rocevic, that we can distinguish between --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during your testimony today, Witness, you mentioned that these people, you were quite clear as to where the people from Rocevic were taken and executed. My question to you is simply: At the time you did not have this information, nor did you know that those people were being -- where those people were taken to be killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's only later that, through rumours flying around, you managed to determine that those people would have been executed, although you never saw that, in the Kozluk area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the time you spent in Rocevic, are you in a position to confirm that the -- by the time you left all the prisoners had been taken away from the Rocevic School on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move to another topic, and that is the -- I will need to move into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So we don't have any questions either for you, sir. Which means that your testimony finishes here. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence in this case. And I also would like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had heard some hinting in Mr. Bourgon's first intervention this morning as to what -- what to expect after this witness's testimony. Do you have any other evidence lined up for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This went quicker than we expected. We -- we do have a witness ready, Ms. Gilleece, who is here and ready. However, I think there is a problem with that in that Mr. Haynes is not here. And I believe that they are -- that team's desire, and I agree with it, was -- was that Mr. Haynes would be dealing with that witness. I don't want to put words in my colleague's mouth. So I'm not sure that we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, or -- I don't know, because I see Mr. Bourgon, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Sarapa, when is Mr. Haynes returning?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He will definitely be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Fauveau? Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Yes, Madam Fauveau. And -- and Mr. Bourgon then.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, okay. All right. My apologies, because I understand, I can follow what she is saying. So it did not occur to me that it was not being translated into English. Basically, she is saying that she is surprised at Mr. Nicholls's intervention because Ms. Gilleece is listed as coming forward to testify on the 5th of February. And the fact that in view of a motion for variance of protective measures, that the Prosecution filed and which we are going to decide here are -- now I am receiving interpretation in French. Okay. Forgiven. We are going to decide that motion of yours for the variation of protective measures in respect to Ms. Gilleece. However, I checked last week with my senior legal officer to see how proximate her testimony was, and initially it was supposed to be this coming -- this coming week, initially I think on the 2nd of February or something like that or on the last day of -- of -- last day of this month or 1st of February because 2nd we are not sitting then I was told it was put off until the 5th. So I think we might as well close the discussion on Ms. Gilleece, except insofar as I can decide -- we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, it's just Because we were expecting Witness 136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are coming to that. Because the next witness, according to what we have been told is PW-143. So I am coming to that. But let's close -- why did you think of bringing forward Ms. Gilleece when we should be talking of witness PW-143, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We sent out a new order. It is true that witness 143 is what we intended to bring next. He is not -- he is here in -- in the -- in town, but he hasn't -- he's not really prepared to testify yet. It's possible that I can try to see if I can get him here by 1.00, but he was not completely -- he hasn't been talked to yet and he's not really ready to go. We thought Ms. Gilleece was a possibility and we, I thought, set that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think Ms. Gilleece is not a possibility at this point in time, as -- as it transpires from your own --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The other reason we brought Ms. Gilleece forward and had her -- brought her out at short notice and got her ready was in the event that Mr. Nikolic was unable to attend, if he had health problems we wanted to have somebody to go. So we got Ms. Gilleece ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. In the meantime, I think we can decide the Prosecution motion for variation of protective measures. Prosecution is seeking the removal of the protective measures that were granted in respect of Ms. Gilleece earlier. The Prosecution request is being granted on the assumption that there is -- would not be any opposition from any of the Defence teams. So all the protective measures granted earlier have now been removed and she can testify publicly. All right. I think this calls for a break now. What I suggest is that we will make ourselves all available in 30 minutes' time and you make every effort, even superhuman efforts, Mr. Nicholls, to try to have PW-143 ready to start giving evidence as soon as possible after the 30-minute break. We are at your disposal. Will you please let us all know that he is ready to start giving evidence and then we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid we do not have a witness available for the rest of the day. I've already made the explanations, so I won't make excuses. We had hoped Ms. Gilleece -- when we brought her, we didn't know that Mr. Haynes was going to be absent when she flew out this weekend. The other witness, I have not been able to bring here and be ready. So I think -- we'd ask the Defence if we could go forward with just the direct, but they do not wish to do that and we respect that. So I'm afraid we do not have another witness for today. We will be ready to start tomorrow on time, and hope -- I don't believe there will be any more gaps. We will try to adjust for this -- this is no criticism, very efficient cross-examination, it's half what we -- the estimate was. That is not a complaint, but it was much quicker than we expected. We will try to keep it moving the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take them one by one with regard to Witness PW-143 and his unavailability today. Is there a real reason why he was not ready, prepared to start his testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's just the schedule of bringing them, Your Honour, and our ability to have them go over their statements and make sure that -- that any disclosure duties we might have going through ISU searches are done and that needs to be completed absolutely before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has the proofing been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have met him Your Honour and had him read his statement. But that's it really because Sunday was the only day and I was with the witness we've just heard for most of the day and worked quite late getting -- getting my disclosure out on that witness, my supplemental information sheet and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That is to an extent understandable on the other hand it is the responsibility of the Trial Chamber to recommend to you as much as possible, particularly based on recent events, to have subsequent witnesses ready to start giving evidence, even in instances like what happened today. In other words, when you have to anticipate their evidence by some hours or a day or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and unfortunately we did that with Ms. Gilleece and we were not able to go ahead with that. We had another witness. We proofed three witnesses yesterday and the third witness is not ready yet and the Defence probably aren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but now I come to Ms. Gilleece. I of course -- my colleagues do understand the concern of at least one of the Defence teams with whom there seems to have been some kind of arrangement already with the Prosecution that he will be present, Mr. Haynes in particular, I'm referring to, when Ms. Gilleece is giving evidence so that he can proceed with his cross-examination. That is understandable, but what we can't understand is the -- this is what we have been told, that there is across the board opposition to having Ms. Gilleece start testifying in chief only with no cross-examinations to follow today. I mean, what's the objection to that? I mean, if she starts her examination-in-chief and hopefully finishes it as well, I mean what's the problem with reserving cross-examinations for all of you until when she returns as scheduled on -- or more or less around the 5th of February? Yes, Mr. McCloskey. It seems that the problem originates more from your side rather than from the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is a particular issue with Mr. Sarapa that we are sensitive to. I don't think the other counsel, I'm not sure, have a problem with the direct only, I know they didn't want to have to cross, which we understand. But there is a unique issue that we've been discussing with Mr. Sarapa, and we really needed Mr. Haynes to be here to avoid that issue. I -- it -- I don't know -- I can -- I, of course, can get into it in more detail, but the practical reality is we should have Mr. Haynes here and that's what Mr. Sarapa wishes and so we're not pushing it beyond that. We were hoping we could do direct, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, but how does Mr. Haynes's presence here affect significantly affect your proceeding with -- with the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Gilleece, when she interviewed General Pandurevic, General Pandurevic had Mr. Sarapa with him at the time, and that is -- has always been known by everyone, and the Registry, and with -- as long as Mr. Haynes was here during that process, there wasn't -- the Registry didn't feel there was a -- a real conflict issue. And so Mr. Sarapa, it's our understanding, feels more comfortable that even direct examination in such a context he would like his counsel to be there -- or his colleague to be there in order to make objections and we understand that. And as I say, that's the situation we find ourselves in. This was many years ago, and he happened to be with -- with the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have discussed, and albeit with some reluctance, because we, as you see, are quite keen, trying to utilise to the best resources that we have. We do, however, understand the respective positions, as explained by Mr. McCloskey, and we agree to postpone the testimony of Ms. Gilleece until later. There are two issues that we would like to address very briefly. Last Friday, Mr. Zivanovic, the Trial Chamber particularly Judge Prost addressed you with respect to your motion for an extension of time regarding the dead-line we imposed on the 17th of January for the Defence filing in relation to the intercept operators.
