And we agreed that we will come back to you today, having had time to think about it, so would you like to address the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I decided nevertheless to remain by our motion, even though we understood your order, and the explanation given by Judge Prost. We believe that we need to present our reasons after all of the witnesses are heard, witnesses concerning the intercepts, including the additional examination of witness Stefanie Frease, which is outstanding. In the meantime the Prosecution was given full access to witness Stefanie Frease. This is why we think that it would be in the interests of the Defence to comply with the order of the Trial Chamber after all of these witnesses are heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's deal with this first. I don't want to give you the impression that this is the first time the four judges have been discussing the merits of Mr. Zivanovic's motion. We have, of course, given it a lot of thought already. Even last Friday, before we decided to address you, Mr. Zivanovic. The position as we see it is the following, and this is the oral decision upon your motion which was filed on the 24th of January and by which you sought an extension beyond the 2nd February 2007 dead-line on the basis, according to you, that this dead-line does not allow the Defence to digest the evidence of various -- all the intercept operators, including that of Ms. Frease. We refer you to our decision of the 17th January, where incidentally we made it abundantly clear that there was a legal, predominantly legal reason why we asked you to, all of you to file a written -- file your written arguments on -- not written arguments, your -- to give notice on your objections to the intercept operators or evidence before the testimony Ms. Frease. There are two -- it was a two-pronged decision. First was that we considered that after having heard several weeks of evidence on this topic the fact that there were a few other witnesses still remaining to be heard on this subject was of no material evidence. We believe that there has been ample opportunity to digest what the substance of the Prosecution case as regards intercept and intercept operator was, and since then we have even heard more intercept operators, so the argument of the Trial Chamber is strengthened. So that stands on its own; should be sufficient to turn down your extension. However, we also wish to deal with your reference of the testimony of Ms. Stefanie Frease. We had made it clear in our decision and also during some exchange of opinions and discussions on this matter, that we needed your broad position on intercepts before the testimony of Ms. Frease precisely because we wanted to avoid the possibility of having Ms. Frease start and finish with her testimony not knowing what your basic objections to the intercepts -- intercept and intercept operator were, with the result that this would be counter-productive for the proper administration of justice in that her testimony could potentially end up with being incomplete, unfinished symphony, if I may call it that. The situation does not change, if anything it now allows for greater weight for the Trial Chamber's argument in that you have heard Ms. Frease give evidence already in two occasions in direct, and you therefore have enough or sufficient information for the time being, what the line she will be pursuing is or will continue to be. So there is no valid argument that we see arising from your submissions and from your motion which could persuade us to grant you an extension. It's a long oral decision, I don't know if the written one would have been shorter. Probably it would have been. So bottom line is, Mr. Zivanovic, your motion is being dismissed. There is also a Prosecution motion requesting protective measures for three witnesses and annexes. You rose one day last week, Mr. Zivanovic, to announce that you had some concerns in relation to one of these witnesses, namely Witness number 143, who would potentially be Witness PW-101. You filed as promised your response last Friday, and we have taken full cognizance of it. Before we proceed with our decisions, after having made consultations, we decided to first make sure if any other Defence team would like to make submissions in relation to the same Prosecution motion, namely in relation to the three witnesses and not just 101, but of course 101, PW-101 included. We hear none. So this is our decision. And again, it is oral and will only be -- and won't be followed by a written decision, unless the Prosecution or the parties indicate they need for one. The Trial Chamber is seized of a Prosecution motion filed on the 24th of January of this year requesting protective measures for three witnesses. And also of a response filed by the Defence team for Mr. Popovic, called Defence Response to Prosecution Motion for Protective Measures for Three Witnesses and Annexes, including ex parte Annex B filed on the 26th of January. We see that the substance of the response by the Popovic Defence team is that the Prosecution, according to the Defence team, has failed to prove that there is a real danger to this witness, 101, PW-101, or Witness 143. We've carefully examined your submissions, we have also carefully examined the Prosecution witness, and in particular the confidential and ex parte reports that have been annexed to the motion, one attached to Annex A dated 10th April 2006, and the other one which is, apart from confidential, also ex parte, which constitutes the substance of Annex B. The Trial Chamber, after having given weight to the information contained particularly in these two annexes, has not the least doubt that the protective measures sought by the Prosecution in their motion are completely justified and we therefore grant the same motion allowing a pseudonym and face distortion of both -- and face distortion for this witness. So I think we have covered all the territory we could cover. Yes, Mr. -- Madam Fauveau. She's always one step ahead of you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to come back on the position of Ms. Frease. She should normally come next Monday. The last schedule we have was the earliest the 8th or the 9th of February. I am a bit concerned by the fact that we are putting in our motion on admissibility; the office will continue to contact her. I am not asking for an extension, but I would request if you could order the Prosecution to cease any contact from the moment we will have filed our motion concerning the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, and then I give you the floor, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Nicholls, I don't know who wishes to address the Trial Chamber on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We do not need to talk to Ms. Frease about what she has testified before, but she's -- she's coming up and we want her testimony to be organised and she's actually assembling the collection of intercepts and that's the -- the significant intercept binders that will form the -- the key exhibit. And this is something we need to -- to talk with her about. I'm not sure what's the purpose of us not talking to Ms. Frease for. I think such an order needs to have -- grounded in some sort of legitimate concern. I don't see it here, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. When do you plan to meet with Ms. Frease? For the proofing, further proofing session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- we see Ms. Frease every day. She's working on a special contract here, and so we see her, you know, frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but seeing her is one thing, proofing her is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Vanderpuye would be the best position to answer that. Usually it would be a day or two in advance, so that is actually -- we have an idea of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's a day or two in advance, and she testifies on Monday, it means you're -- have the proofing sessions on Saturday and Sunday. If you see her every day, I mean, why can't that take place before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are open to the Court's suggestions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not coming with suggestions, I'm just asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We try to do it a day or two before so that you know that it's going to happen. And -- because as you know, schedules change and there's so much work to be done. So I would have to get to Mr. Vanderpuye to get -- to get you better information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The bottom line is that we are not giving you a decision on this now. We decided to continue discussing, deliberating on this between today and tomorrow and we'll come back to you tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Bourgon was before. Unless -- unless it's on the same subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It may be, Mr. President. We just like to let you know that we fully agree with the objection of Ms. Fauveau. We think it's -- be highly inappropriate to act otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we also support the motion by my colleague, Mrs. Fauveau. Now, maybe there is another way around it, to simply -- that we can file our submissions ex parte until the end of the testimony of Mrs. Frease. We really feel that it is something that would be inappropriate because our submissions are very much likely -- are very likely to address the issues that will come up in her testimony, and we feel it's inappropriate for the Prosecution to have the benefit of those submissions and even if it is not a question of preparation. If it is only to prepare the way they will tailor the examination-in-chief or what is left of it. For this purpose we would much prefer if we could simply file ex parte until she -- once she's finished her testimony. This way the Trial Chamber gets what the Trial Chamber is interested in. You will know exactly what is each of our respective positions with respect to the admissibility and the arguments that we may have on the intercepts. At the same time we proceed in a fair manner by having the Prosecution proceed with -- with a normal examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to hear the justification for this. If -- if the Defence has issues with the intercepts we would like to hear them as they are obligated to provide -- their Defence, they're obligated to provide certain issues so the Prosecution may deal with them so that we don't go into this back and forth. So I don't understand the gamesmanship going on here, and I haven't seen a reason for the gamesmanship. If there's a reason, you know, I'm -- I'm no adversarial warrior but I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the position of the Defence with respect to the intercept was laid out in each of our own pre-trial briefs and the Prosecution knows what the overall position is. Whether it's been explained enough for my colleague is a different matter, but the issue is, we've already said that we are disputing the admissibility of the intercepts. That should be enough for our colleague to understand what he wants. The Trial Chamber would like the benefit for more detailed explanation, of course we go do that because we have been ordered to do that and it will be our pleasure to do it, but we feel it will be inappropriate for those submissions, those detailed submissions to precede the final examination-in-chief of Ms. Frease. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution confirm that Witness 170 will be giving evidence before Ms. Frease is available for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When we figure out who that is, we should have an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: According to the last schedule I have seen, that is the position, but we were a little concerned from what was being said that things may have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what sense, that things may have changed in the sense that Ms. Frease will testify before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the case? I suppose you can verify this. We are not talking about a month ahead or two months ahead, we are talking of a few days ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is our plan and I will talk to my colleague and talk to everybody, but that is -- the concern he expressed, I don't think he's going to have anything to worry about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just to emphasise, Your Honour, Witness 170 is particularly pertinent to our client and our case. That's why we have this concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we will -- yes, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Bourgon, because it's perhaps most directly related to your comments, perhaps you could explain a little better to me or to us the position that you are taking with respect to these arguments on the intercepts. The Prosecution is proffering certain evidence which they would like to be admitted. The Defence have indicated they are objecting to that evidence, but basically that's the essence of it, that there is an objection to evidence otherwise which would be admissable. And your suggestion is that the Prosecution should therefore present its evidence without any additional information as to why, what the basis of the objection is, that the Prosecution in essence should bring forward evidence trying to guess as to what the basis for the objections is. I don't quite understand why we are not to get the benefit of knowing at least the underlying objection so that the evidence we hear will be relevant to those objections instead of simply every possible kind of argument that the Prosecution might try and understand to be the basis for the objection. I am a little unclear as to why the Defence is opposed to at least indicating the basis of their objection. Perhaps you could address us on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Of course I can only speak on behalf of the client we respect in this case. As far as we are concerned contesting the admissibility of exhibits, there's not too many things you can do to challenge the admissibility. As far as we're concerned, we are challenging the admissibility on the basis of a total lack of reliability. Our questions so far have been addressed on the reliability aspects of the intercept. This is what we will detail in our motion that, in our submission, that the Trial Chamber has asked for. There has been no secret, my colleague knows exactly that this is what we will be explaining. What we simply want is not to detail every one of our arguments that go to reliability before they have the last witness, to me which is the most important witness, who can maybe patch up lack of reliability. It's as simple as that. If the Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecution is entitled to know what the Defence arguments are ahead of time as to why it is totally -- a total absence of reliability, then we will -- we will of course -- we will abide by the Trial Chamber's order. Now, this is the position of this team. I know that other teams might have different reason to challenge admissibility. As far as we are concerned, reliability is -- is one of the issues that must be taken into consideration, and we are of the view that it is a complete absence of reliability. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One further question. Do you mean to say then by supporting or joining in the request of Madam Fauveau that you wouldn't like a situation where the Prosecution can proof Ms. Frease on reliability issues simply because -- because that would -- would go against your rights or whatever? What -- I can't follow the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if you yourself are say that there will be no details forthcoming, and we had made it also clear in our explanation to you that what we are requiring from you for the time being is a broad overview for the basis for your motion, let's call it that, on the admissibility of intercepts, and the question of reliability in general is being proffered by you, why shouldn't Mr. McCloskey know it before he proofs Ms. Frease for the purpose of her continued examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you prefer a situation where he doesn't know that you will be -- admittedly now he knows, but do you want a situation to obtain where he doesn't know that you are contesting the reliability of this evidence with the result that he will not proof Ms. Frease on that issue, and then we come -- we come here, perhaps even finish with her testimony, and then all of a sudden we find ourselves faced with a whole list of arguments dealing with the substance of -- of your objection as to the admissibility? I mean, I don't know, but let's not discuss it any further. We hear what you have to say on this and then we come back tomorrow because we have agreed that it deserves a little more thought and discussion than we have been able to give it here in the few minutes that we have available. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In short, Mr. President, the Prosecution has the onus when asking for exhibits to be admitted on evidence to show that both probative value and that inside probative value reliability is included and we from the beginning have said that these exhibits have a complete absence of reliability. That is why we will argue that they are inadmissible. In our submission to the Trial Chamber at this stage explain every detail, that is what we will do in our submission. So I'm not sure when I saw what you said about no details, in the contrary, we will put lots of details in that submission as to why there is no reliability. So the Trial Chamber knows exactly where we are going. Then my colleague, knowing that this is our position on reliability, then he knows what he has to do and the onus is on him to show that these intercepts are reliable. We don't see why we should be helping the Prosecution to show the Prosecution, my colleague, I'm sure, knows exactly what he has to do to show that the intercepts are reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I doubt in my mind is how that fits in with your previous statement that we made even now the a decision of 17 January that we needed this position or declaration of position from your part, before the testimony of Ms. Frease. That was one of the basic reasons why we handed down our decision the way we did. Yes, let's hear Mr. McCloskey first, and then you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I make a comment to Mr. Bourgon before we go further? The problem, as I understand on the part of Defence is the -- the opposition you are now going raise is related to not only the admissibility of certain documents, but also to the Defence case, finally that goes to the reliability or weight of the Defence -- the Prosecution witness in a sense. If the document is to be admitted at all. So what we want you to produce is not a detailed opposition, what we want to know is just crux, skeleton opposition on the part of the Defence. To the extent, not to reveal the Defence case, which can be raised again in a more detailed manner later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. In that case what I have mentioned this morning is what will be in our submission and then we are absolutely -- we misunderstood and we apologise. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's quite interesting. First we have a statement from that you, you shouldn't -- you wouldn't like the Prosecution to be aware of your position before they -- or while they are proofing Ms. Frease, and now you tell the Prosecution as from now what your position is going to be before they have even started proofing Ms. Frease, but anyway you don't need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: They have known from the beginning what our position has been. Maybe they have other questions for other Defence teams but as far as we are going, it's very easy to tell where we're going by the questions we've been asking. And the Prosecution knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey and then Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I read it, I may be wrong, but I believe the Defence wants to be able to bring up for example a specific intercept and a specific problem that shows this intercept is not reliable, doesn't want it to be tagged so when Ms. Frease can come in and she us why she thinks they're wrong. I think that's what they are saying. If that's the case, I believe we're always going to be able to respond to the Defence and their factual arguments either in a rebuttal case or in our own case, be that -- it -- recalling Ms. Frease to deal with issues or having it -- dealt with people, why such a detailed attack on our intercepts is something we shouldn't see at this point. It seems to be unnecessary, but the Prosecution does want to be able to respond to their detailed attack, and we expect a detailed attack. And we don't need to do it now, but I'm sure this system allows for us to respond one way or another. As the Court is aware, rebuttal evidence, the law on rebuttal evidence is if the Prosecutor could have put it in his case in chief, he can't bring rebuttal. And, of course, God only knows how much we could put in our case in chief, perhaps not much more on intercept evidence. But, so rebuttal evidence is difficult especially with the -- we can all imagine the end of this trial, rebuttal evidence is the last thing anyone is going to want to consider, is my guess. But we do want to have the ability to respond to Defence counsel and their -- and their detailed attack, and I'm sure this Court will allow it one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Ms. Fauveau, would you like to round it up?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. When I raised this objection I was not sufficiently clear and I have not perhaps presented enough arguments to support my thesis. I will be very direct. By presenting to the Chamber my arguments concerning the non-admissibility of the intercepts, I will -- when I address the Chamber, I will talk about the cross-examination of Mrs. Frease, and this is what I would like to avoid; this is why I agree fully with Mr. Bourgon. Maybe it can be filed ex parte up until Mrs. Frease begins her testimony, or before she begins her testimony, or to stop the contacts with Mrs. Frease and the Prosecutor regarding intercepted conversation or intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we've heard enough. As I said, we'll come back tomorrow afternoon when we resume our sitting, our hearing, after having had time to go deeper into this issue. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On a different issue, which is what I wanted to raise before, the last issue on the intercept. And that deals with -- the Trial Chamber has just rendered a decision concerning protective measures for Witness PW-101. This decision was rendered on the basis of inter parte submissions but also on the basis of ex parte submissions. This is without being exactly sure, this is at least the third time that we are dealing in this case with ex parte submissions. Mr. President, we fail to understand why we have to live with ex parte submissions. We have -- there is an outstanding motion as you know, which deals with one witness that we don't even know not only the name, the identification, we don't even know what the witness will be speaking about. There is a motion for this witness to be accepted on the Prosecution's list. We are just simply raising the issue. We feel that we are heading in a dangerous path, and that there is too much ex parte submissions going on without the Defence being informed. Maybe there is a reason for that, but we see our role as Defence counsel, as officers of the court, that we have duties and obligations not to reveal information that we come across in submissions that are filed confidentially, and that we have also addressed in our motion that there might be other remedies short of doing a full ex parte submission, so that we may know when we have the information on which decisions are rendered which affect the rights of our clients. I just raise this as an issue at this time because we are a bit afraid that this is an ongoing process of taking the ex parte route when this is not necessary when dealing with the Defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just in relation, Your Honours, I'll just say that I think that the ex parte filings we've made, I think, on their face it can be seen why they're ex parte. We don't try to file anything ex parte unless necessary. It's something available to both parties, we under if they on occasion need to file pleadings in an ex parte -- on an ex parte basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to make something clear that part of your submission seems to indicate that the Defence was not informed that included or annexed to the Prosecution motion there was an ex parte confidential and ex parte Annex B. Mr. Zivanovic's motion itself refers to Annex B, although I am of course aware that none of the Defence teams were is privy to the contents of ex parte Annex B. The procedure as it is, is what it is, and namely the ex parte availability or remedy is of extreme importance when it comes to the personal safety to the life and limb of certain individuals, and of course the -- the whole thing is based on the assumption that the Trial Chamber, who is -- comes -- becomes familiar to the content of an ex parte filing acts responsibly. Everything is based on this assumption. I don't think that there is reason to doubt that. On the other hand I also wish to state that compared to other cases in which I have been involved in, at least the number of ex parte filings in this case have been pretty much limited. There is no reason, at least I speak for myself, I would need to consult with my clients -- my colleagues. Sorry. I have revealed my background as Defence counsel before I became a judge in my country. There is no reason for us to intervene in any of the cases that we have heard so far on the basis that the Prosecution abused of its right or possibility to file ex parte filings. And there have been ex parte filings also on the part of the Defence, incidentally, and also there we do not see any reason -- we never saw any reason for intervening. Yes, we filled the time and we're finishing five minutes before. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe we can fill the five minutes. Your Honour, just there were two exhibits with the witness that -- in the rush at the end I neglected to tender, if could I do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's our fault as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first is P0244 which is simply the pseudonym sheet under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that is admitted. No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the second is number 1690, that was the one photograph of the building which I showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are there any objections? I hear none. So that is also admitted. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to help clarify one scheduling matter, we had -- to take up the extra space, we had brought in for this week expert Helga Brunborg on the demography and the missing. We have been in touch with the Nikolic team on that and they are -- they have their own expert and they have asked that it be direct examination only, which we have agreed with, though -- and I believe the other Defence team are on board with that. But I just wanted -- the plan right now, as far as we know, is direct examination only for Mr. Brunborg, and so if everybody agrees we will put that into the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What I suggest is the following,

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First that you approach Mr. Josse in relation to Witness 170 and explain to him your position, supposedly to allay his concerns, as you put it. The second is speaking for myself, I am beginning to have some kind of confusion in my mind as to the scheduling of witnesses for the next two weeks or until we come to the break. If you could perhaps file formally or informally a schedule of witnesses to be heard between now and when we have the short recess starting on the 12th. All right? And we are not sitting on the 2nd because that's maintenance, court maintenance day. Thank you. We will reconvene tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
